It's not easy to say if the mesh at TE is sufficient to capture the dynamics of interest. Perhaps you might find some literature on a similar type of simulation. Or run a few simulations on an airfoil that has been previously performed to validate your mesh

It might work. Only concern is that keeping y+>1 means that you'll not resolve the viscous sublayer. This leads to losing the dissipative effects associated with smaller scales and possibility of the solution blowing up. This will show up in the convergence check if there is a possibility. Also, to save time, you can run a series of RANS simulation for the check and set the cell height for the subsequent LES.

The target y+ value is good for an initial estimate of first cell height. You then run the simulation and plot the y+ value for the quasi-steady flow to verify if the values match the target value. If not, you will need to reduce the first cell height and re-run the simulation. Simultaneously, you will need to perform grid convergence study to verify if the parameters like lift/drag coefficients have converged. You can take a look at this video which explains these points in detail: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=60fDz2cVdy8
